name: Crisóstomo Ibarra (later "Simoun")
summary: A young, European-educated mestizo who returns to San Diego hoping to reform his country through education. Years later he resurfaces in Manila as the wealthy, embittered jeweler Simoun.
details: Ibarra spent seven years studying in Europe, returning to San Diego with progressive ideas about education and reform. His homecoming reception at Capitán Tiago's house became infamous when Padre Dámaso openly insulted him — a sign of the deep social tensions between the Spanish friars and the Filipino ilustrados. After his father's death and his own persecution, Ibarra fakes his death and returns in the sequel novel El Filibusterismo as the mysterious jeweler Simoun, seeking revenge through revolution.

name: Capitán Tiago
summary: A wealthy, socially anxious Filipino elite who hosted Ibarra's homecoming reception. Maria Clara's legal father.
details: Don Santiago de los Santos, known as Capitán Tiago, is one of the wealthiest men in Manila. He hosted the dinner reception for Ibarra's return, but his social anxieties and desire to please both Spanish authorities and Filipino elites made him a complicated figure in colonial society. His mansion was the setting for one of the novel's most dramatic scenes — Padre Dámaso's public insult of Ibarra.

name: Padre Dámaso
summary: An arrogant Franciscan friar and former San Diego parish priest, openly hostile to Ibarra at the reception dinner despite once being close to Ibarra's late father.
details: Padre Dámaso was the parish priest of San Diego for many years and was close to Ibarra's father, Don Rafael. However, after Don Rafael's death, Dámaso's attitude changed dramatically. At Ibarra's homecoming reception, he was openly rude and hostile — shocking the other guests and revealing the deep power dynamics between Spanish friars and the Filipino community. Dámaso represents the corrupt and abusive Spanish friar class that Rizal criticized in his novel.

name: Mang Tenyo
summary: A cart driver who gives the player their cover identity as a visiting scholar's aide from Manila. The first friendly face in San Diego.
details: Mang Tenyo represents the everyday Filipino townsfolk of 1887 — observant, cautious, and quietly aware of the social tensions around them. His warning not to mention the Ibarra name too loudly hints at how deeply Padre Dámaso's outburst affected the community. In a town where speaking against the friars could mean exile or imprisonment, even casual gossip carries weight.

name: Maria Clara
summary: Ibarra's beloved — the beautiful, devout daughter of Capitán Tiago. She symbolizes the ideal Filipino woman of the colonial era.
details: Maria Clara de los Santos y Alba is the fiancée of Crisóstomo Ibarra and the legal daughter of Capitán Tiago. She is beautiful, devout, and seemingly perfect — but her story reveals the constraints placed on Filipino women by colonial society and the Catholic Church. She represents the 'ideal woman' that colonial society expected: obedient, religious, and subservient. Later revelations about her true parentage add tragic depth to her character.

name: Aling Nena
summary: A kitchen worker at Capitán Tiago's household who witnessed the reception drama firsthand. One of the gossip sources in the market.
details: Aling Nena works in Capitán Tiago's kitchen and was present during the infamous dinner reception. Her gossip about what happened provides the player with crucial insight into how Ibarra's homecoming was disrupted by Padre Dámaso's behavior. She represents the common people who witnessed the abuses of the friar class.

name: Mang Andres
summary: A local vendor who trades near the market stalls. He overheard the reception drama and provides additional gossip context.
details: Mang Andres is a market vendor who trades goods near the San Diego town plaza. He heard about the drama at Capitán Tiago's reception and can confirm the details that Aling Nena shares. His perspective as a tradesman highlights how colonial-era gossip and social dynamics affected even the simplest interactions in the marketplace.

name: San Diego (Town)
summary: The fictional town where much of Noli Me Tangere takes place — Rizal's composite of typical Philippine towns under Spanish colonial rule.
details: San Diego is not a real town but a fictional composite. Rizal used it to represent the typical Philippine town of the 1880s — with its church, convent, plaza, market, and the social hierarchy that defined colonial life. The town's name ('Saint Didacus') reflects the Spanish Catholic influence. In the novel, San Diego is where Ibarra's family estate is located, and where many of the key events of the story unfold.

name: Town Plaza
summary: The central gathering place of San Diego — where the church, market, and Ibarra mansion all face. A hub of social life and gossip.
details: In colonial Philippine towns, the plaza was the center of everything. It connected the church (representing Spanish spiritual authority), the government buildings (representing Spanish political authority), and the market (representing Filipino economic life). The layout itself was a physical map of colonial power dynamics. The San Diego plaza is where Ibarra is seen crossing after his return, and where gossip about the reception spreads fastest.

name: The Ilustrados
summary: The educated Filipino class who studied in Europe and brought back reformist ideas — Ibarra (and Rizal himself) exemplify this group.
details: The ilustrados ('enlightened ones') were Filipino students and professionals who studied in Spain, France, Germany, and other European countries in the late 1800s. They were exposed to liberal ideas, secular education, and political reform movements. When they returned to the Philippines, they were viewed with suspicion by Spanish colonial authorities and the friars, who feared their calls for equality and representation. José Rizal himself was an ilustrado, and Crisóstomo Ibarra is his fictional counterpart in the novel.

name: José Rizal
summary: The author of Noli Me Tangere (1887) — a Filipino nationalist, novelist, and reformist whose works helped inspire the Philippine Revolution.
details: José Protasio Rizal Mercado y Alonso Realonda (1861–1896) wrote Noli Me Tangere in Spanish, publishing it in Berlin in 1887. The novel exposed the abuses of Spanish colonial rule, particularly the power of the friars. Rizal was executed by firing squad on December 30, 1896, on charges of rebellion, sedition, and conspiracy — an event that catalyzed the Philippine Revolution. He is now the national hero of the Philippines.

name: Noli Me Tangere (The Novel)
summary: José Rizal's 1887 novel that exposed Spanish colonial abuses in the Philippines. Its title is Latin for 'Touch me not'.
details: Noli Me Tangere was published in Berlin, Germany in 1887. The title comes from the Latin words Jesus spoke to Mary Magdalene after the Resurrection. The novel follows Crisóstomo Ibarra's return to the Philippines after seven years in Europe, and depicts the corruption and abuses of the Spanish friars and colonial officials. The book was banned in the Philippines but circulated secretly, becoming a catalyst for the reform movement and eventual revolution.

name: Spanish Colonial Philippines
summary: The 333-year period when Spain ruled the Philippines (1565–1898), during which friars held enormous social, political, and economic power.
details: The Spanish colonial period in the Philippines lasted from 1565 to 1898. During this time, the Catholic friar orders (Dominicans, Franciscans, Augustinians, and Jesuits) held enormous power — not just spiritual, but also political and economic. They controlled education, land ownership, and local governance. Padre Dámaso in Noli Me Tangere represents this friar class, whose abuses were a central theme of Rizal's critique. The colonial structure placed Spaniards above Filipino elites (like Capitán Tiago), who were above the common people, creating a rigid social hierarchy.

name: Filipinismo (Filipino Identity)
summary: The emerging sense of Filipino national identity in the 1880s — the idea that Filipinos were a distinct people with their own culture and rights, not merely Spanish subjects.
details: Filipinismo was the cultural and political awakening that defined the late 19th century in the Philippines. Before this period, most Filipinos identified primarily with their local town or province, not as a unified nation. The ilustrados, through their European education and exposure to liberal ideas, began to articulate a sense of shared Filipino identity. Rizal's novels were instrumental in this process — by depicting Filipino characters with depth and dignity, he challenged the Spanish narrative that Filipinos were inferior subjects.
